## Paper

## Abstract

Rechargeable aqueous batteries show promise for large-scale energy storage, yet suffer from low specific energy and poor low-temperature performance. Existing low-temperature aqueous batteries typically use ion-insertion positive electrodes with limited capacity. While aqueous sulfur-based batteries offer high theoretical capacity, their low-temperature operation remains challenging. Current improvement strategies often compromise room-temperature performance due to the inclusion of non-active additives. Here, we present a low-temperature sulfur-based battery using a Cu(BF4)2-based electrolyte, which boasts a low glass transition temperature of −115.1 °C, and an ionic conductivity of 5.16 mS cm−1 at −60 °C. This electrolyte enables faster reaction kinetics and higher overall specific energy than traditional CuSO4-based systems. The resulting zinc-sulfur battery delivers a discharge capacity of 348 mAh g−1 and an specific energy of 339 Wh kg−1 at −50 °C, based on the total mass of both the positive and negative electrodes, competitive with existing aqueous batteries.

---

## Introduction

Large-scale energy storage systems are essential for integrating renewable energy sources like wind and solar power into the grid1,2. Among various storage technologies, rechargeable aqueous batteries standout due to their safety, cost-effectiveness, and environmental advantages3–5. However, the practical application of aqueous batteries is currently limited by two major challenges: (i) low specific energy and (ii) poor electrochemical performance at low temperatures6,7. Despite significant efforts, the development of low-temperature aqueous batteries with high specific energy remains largely unrealized.

In current low-temperature aqueous batteries, positive electrodes typically rely on ion insertion and extraction mechanisms8–13. However, these systems are often limited by relatively low capacities, frequently falling below 200 mAh g−1 at low temperatures. This limitation underscores the need for the development of low-temperature aqueous batteries capable of achieving higher discharge capacities. Positive electrode materials based on conversion reactions generally offer higher specific capacities compared to ion-insertion-based counterparts. Among these, sulfur, a well-established conversion-reaction positive electrode, has been investigated for use in aqueous batteries, demonstrating a high theoretical capacity of 3350 mAh g−1 based on a four-electron conversion mechanism14. This represents the highest specific capacity achieved for any positive electrode materials. Despite these promising advancements, existing aqueous sulfur-based batteries typically employ 0.5 m copper sulfate as the electrolyte15–18, which exhibits limited anti-freezing ability, thus restricting their applicability in extreme environments such as high-altitude, deep-space, and deep-sea conditions. Thus, the development of low-temperature sulfur-based batteries is highly desirable.

The development of anti-freezing aqueous electrolytes compatible with four-electron sulfur positive electrodes is crucial. So far, various strategies have been adopted in the design of low-temperature-tolerant electrolytes, such as the utilization of high-concentration electrolytes19,20, organic additives21,22, and anti-freeze hydrogel electrolytes23,24. However, these approaches often lead to trade-offs, such as reduced ionic conductivity, compromised safety, or diminished specific energy due to the incorporation of non-electrochemically active additives. Consequently, there is a pressing need to improve the anti-freezing performance of aqueous electrolytes without sacrificing their ionic conductivity or adversely affecting the overall specific energy and safety of the battery system.

Here, we identify redox-active 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2, which exhibits a low glass transition temperature of −115.1 °C and a high ionic conductivity of 5.16 mS cm−1 at −60 °C. Comprehensive spectral analysis and molecular dynamics simulations show that BF4− anions can significantly disrupt the existing hydrogen bond (HB) network among water molecules, resulting in robust low-temperature resistance. Compared with traditional 0.5 m CuSO4 electrolyte, the 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte endows the sulfur positive electrode with faster reaction kinetics, better rate performance (1575 mAh g−1 at 20 A g−1), and higher specific energy. In addition, the prepared zinc-sulfur (Zn–S) full cells provided a high discharge specific capacity of 1767 mAh g−1 and an specific energy of up to 1724 Wh kg−1 at −50 °C, competitive with the performance of current low-temperature aqueous batteries. This work introduces the four-electron sulfur positive electrode into low-temperature aqueous battery systems, thereby providing a promising pathway for large-scale low-temperature energy storage applications. Crucially, this study overcomes the limitations of traditional anti-freezing additives, which, while improve the anti-freezing ability, often compromise the electrochemical performance and energy efficiency of aqueous systems.

---

## Results

S@CNT positive electrode preparation and anti-freezing electrolytes design
To improve the electronic conductivity of sulfur and alleviate its volume expansion during the discharge process, carbon nanotubes (CNTs) were used as the host for sulfur. The scanning electron microscope (SEM) image of CNTs is shown in Supplementary Fig. 1. A melt diffusion method was used to synthesize S@CNT composite. X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern of the composite exhibits peaks consistent with crystalline sulfur (Supplementary Fig. 2a), and the thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) shows the sulfur content in the composite is 63% by mass (Supplementary Fig. 2b). Elemental mappings confirm the sulfur is evenly distributed throughout the CNT host (Supplementary Fig. 3).

A critical challenge in developing low-temperature sulfur-based batteries is the creation of a low-temperature-tolerant copper ion electrolyte that remains compatible with sulfur positive electrodes. In previously reported aqueous four-electron sulfur-based batteries, copper sulfate (CuSO4, 0.5 m) was commonly used as the electrolyte14–18. To evaluate the low-temperature performance, we investigated the anti-freezing properties of copper sulfate solutions at various concentrations. As shown in Supplementary Figs. 4 and 5, differential scanning calorimeter (DSC) measurements indicate that the freezing points of various concentrations of CuSO4 are above −10 °C, which severely impedes the Cu2+ transfer process and limits the battery performance at low temperatures. Therefore, copper sulfate solutions are unsuitable as electrolytes for low-temperature applications.

Introducing HB acceptors into the water to break its original HB network is an effective strategy for improving the anti-freezing ability of the solution21. Fluorine (F), with high electronegativity, acts as a suitable HB acceptor, facilitating the O−H∙∙∙F interaction with water molecules25. The tetrafluoroborate anion (BF4−), with four B−F bonds, is capable of forming multiple HBs with water, greatly disrupting the original HB network between water molecules. Furthermore, compared to other chaotropic anions such as ClO4− and TFSI−, Cu(BF4)2 exhibits a significant cost advantage (Supplementary Fig. 6). This makes Cu(BF4)2 a promising copper ion electrolyte for low-temperature aqueous sulfur-based batteries.

As shown in Fig. 1a, keep at −60 °C, Cu(BF4)2 solutions with low concentrations (1–2 m) freeze, while those with high concentrations (3-5 m) remain liquid, indicating that the anti-freezing ability of Cu(BF4)2 solution is influenced by its concentration. The phase transition behaviors of Cu(BF4)2 at different concentrations was further studied using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) (Supplementary Fig. 7). As the concentration of Cu(BF4)2 increases, the phase transition temperature initially decreases and then increases, and 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 delivers the lowest glass transition temperature of −115 °C (Fig. 1b).

In addition, ion conductivity at low temperatures is crucial for constructing high-performance low-temperature aqueous batteries. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was used to study the ionic conductivity of different concentrations of Cu(BF4)2 solutions at different temperatures (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 8). At 25 °C, there is little difference in ionic conductivity across different concentrations. But as the temperature drops to −40 °C, 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 shows higher ion conductivity and maintains an ion conductivity of 5.16 mS cm−1 at −60 °C, competitive with previously reported low-temperature electrolytes (Fig. 1d)8,19,22,26–28. While the concentration is greater than 3.5 m, the ionic conductivity decreases, which could be due to the increase in electrolyte viscosity (Supplementary Fig. 9). To further investigate the temperature dependence of ion conductivity, the activation energy of conductivity in Cu(BF4)2 solutions at various concentrations was calculated using the Arrhenius equation29 (Supplementary Fig. 10). The activation energy, which governs the ion conductivity-temperature relationship19, was found to be lowest in the 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 solution at 0.24 eV (Fig. 1e), indicating good low-temperature ionic conductivity and temperature stability.

Anti-freezing mechanism of electrolyte
To comprehensively understand the mechanism behind the anti-freezing ability of the Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte, Raman spectra of Cu(BF4)2 solutions at different concentrations were collected (Supplementary Fig. 11a). The peak at ~767 cm−1 is attributed to the stretching vibration of the B−F bond, which gradually becomes stronger with the increase of the Cu(BF4)2 concentration (Supplementary Fig. 11b)30,31. The O–H stretching vibration of water typically occurs in the range of 2900–3800 cm−1 (see refs. 32,33), which can be deconvoluted into three components corresponding to three types of HBs: strong HBs (~3200 cm−1), weak HBs (~3400 cm−1), and non-HBs (~3600 cm−1). With increasing Cu(BF4)2 concentration, the peak intensity attributed to non-HBs rises (Fig. 2a), indicating a strengthened interaction between BF4− anions and water molecules25,34. This is further supported by the observation that the proportion of non-HBs increases while that of strong HBs decreases (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 12). In contrast, CuSO4 solutions show only minor variations in peak intensity with changing concentration (Supplementary Fig. 13), suggesting a negligible enhancement of non-HB interactions. These results collectively demonstrate that Cu(BF4)2 progressively disrupts the HB network among water molecules.

Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectra provide additional confirmation of the evolution of the HB structure in the Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte (Supplementary Fig. 14). The stretching vibration of the B−F bonds shifts to lower wavenumbers (redshift) with increasing Cu(BF4)2 concentration (Supplementary Fig. 15), which is attributed to the enhanced interaction between the H atoms of water molecules and the F atoms of the BF4− anions35. Similarly, fitting the O−H stretching region and deconvoluting it into three components (Supplementary Fig. 16 and 17) shows that the proportion of non-HBs increases with Cu(BF4)2 concentration, consistent with the Raman spectroscopy results. Therefore, the introduction of BF4− significantly disrupts the original HB network in water, suppressing ice crystal nucleation and improving the anti-freezing ability.

To investigate the anti-freezing mechanism of the electrolyte, theoretical simulations were also performed. The results reveal that although SO42− exhibits stronger interaction with water molecules than BF4− (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. 18), it is the BF4−-based electrolyte that demonstrates good anti-freezing performance. This can be attributed to their distinct influences on the HB network of water. SO42−, with its high charge density, strongly binds to H2O via ion-dipole interactions, leading to the formation of a highly ordered and stable hydration shell (Fig. 2d). This ordered structure consequently strengthens the long-range HB network of water, facilitating ice formation. In contrast, BF4− shows weaker binding energy with water molecules, which prevents the formation of an ordered hydration shell, leading instead to a loose and flexible hydration structure (Fig. 2d). This disruption of the extended HB connectivity effectively inhibits the water molecular arrangement necessary for freezing. Therefore, the anti-freezing performance of the aqueous electrolyte is determined by the ability to disrupt the global HB network, rather than the strength of the local bonding energy between the two species.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were used to investigate the structure of Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte at different concentrations (Supplementary Fig. 19). As the concentration increases, the number of HBs among water molecules decreases monotonically (Supplementary Fig. 20). This trend appears to contradict the V-shaped phase transition temperature, which reaches a minimum at 3.5 m. This can be understood from an entropic perspective. As demonstrated by Mai et al.11,12, increasing salt concentration introduces two competing effects: the disruption of the water HB network increases entropy, while the enhanced ion-water and ion-ion interactions decrease it. The balance of these opposing effects results in an optimal concentration—in this case, 3.5 m—where the phase transition temperature is minimized. Structural analysis at this optimal concentration provides further insight: in 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2, the proportion of HBs between water molecules drops to 33.5%, compared to 70.6% in the 1 m system, whereas the ratios of H2O−BF4− and H2O−Cu2+ increased substantially (Fig. 2e). Besides, each F atom in BF4− can form H-bonds with multiple neighboring H2O molecules (Supplementary Fig. 21), resulting in a higher ratio of H2O−BF4− interactions compared to H2O−Cu2+, suggesting BF4− plays a predominant role in improving the anti-freezing ability of the electrolyte. Additionally, further kinetic analysis through mean squared displacement (MSD) calculations shows that water molecules in the 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte exhibits a lower diffusion coefficient (1.51 × 10−5 m2 s−1) compared to 1 m system (4.26 × 10−5 m2 s−1) (Fig. 2f). This slowdown can be attributed to the enhanced H2O−BF4− (or Cu2+) interactions in the electrolyte.

The enhanced reaction kinetic of positive electrode
In addition to exhibiting anti-freezing performance, 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte also enhances the reaction kinetics of the sulfur positive electrode. Compared to traditional CuSO4 electrolytes, 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte shows enhancement in both rate performance and specific energy. To evaluate this, we compared the electrochemical performance of the sulfur positive electrode in different electrolytes, including 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 and 0.5 m CuSO4 electrolytes. The Cu|3.5 m Cu(BF4)2|S@CNT coin cell demonstrated good rate performance, delivering high specific capacities of 1697, 1679, and 1575 mAh g−1 even at high specific current of 5, 10, and 20 A g−1, respectively (Fig. 3a, b). In contrast, the Cu|0.5 m CuSO4|S@CNT cell only achieved specific capacities of 1327, 1011, and 492 mAh g−1 at the same specific current, showing a distinct advantage for the 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte. Furthermore, we also compared the polarization of the cells based on 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 and 0.5 m CuSO4 electrolytes at different specific current. The cells with 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte exhibited lower polarization, with values of 0.102, 0.127, 0.176, and 0.263 V at specific current of 2, 5, 10, and 20 A g−1 (Supplementary Figs. 22–24), respectively. Notably, compared to the traditional 0.5 m CuSO4 electrolyte, the 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte enhances the specific energy of the Cu–S@CNT cell. The specific energy improvement becomes more pronounced with increasing specific current, reaching 203% at 20 A g−1 (Fig. 3c). Moreover, the Cu|3.5 m Cu(BF4)2|S@CNT cell also exhibits stable cycling performance, maintaining 91% capacity retention after 400 cycles at 5 A g−1 (Supplementary Fig. 25). Furthermore, comparative rate performance analysis shows that Cu(BF4)2 electrolytes across different concentrations exhibit enhanced kinetics compared to the 0.5 m CuSO4 (Supplementary Fig. 26).

To investigate the mechanism behind the improved rate performance, we systematically characterized the electrochemical properties of the electrolyte systems. The ionic conductivity of the 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte at 25 °C was measured to be 100.3 mS cm−1, significantly higher than the 21.8 mS cm−1 observed for the 0.5 m CuSO4 electrolyte (Supplementary Figs. 27–29). Charge transfer impedance (Rct) was used to evaluate the diffusion resistance of ions at the electrolyte-electrode interface, a crucial factor influencing the rate performance of the cell. We measured the Rct of Cu–S@CNT cell with two different electrolytes at different voltages and found that the Rct for the cell with 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 was significantly lower than that with 0.5 m CuSO4 (Supplementary Figs. 30 and 31 and Supplementary Table 1). Galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) is also used to study the diffusion kinetics of Cu2+ in the electrode material, revealing higher diffusion coefficients with 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte compared to 0.5 m CuSO4 electrolyte (Supplementary Fig. 32). The enhanced performance of the 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte is further evidenced by its higher Cu2+ transference number (0.698) compared to the 0.5 m CuSO4 electrolyte (Supplementary Figs. 33 and 34). MD simulations were conducted to investigate the origin of this enhanced Cu2+ transport (Supplementary Fig. 35).

The solvation structure of the electrolyte plays a critical role in desolvation kinetics36–38, which in turn determines reaction kinetics. Thus, we systematically compared the solvation structures of the two electrolytes. The high binding energy between Cu2+–BF4−, Cu2+–SO42− suggested that BF4− and SO42− ions can preferentially participate in the solvation sheath of Cu2+ in electrolytes (Fig. 3d). The radial distribution function (RDF) analysis of 0.5 m CuSO4 reveals negligible participation of SO42− in the primary solvation shell of Cu2+ at this low concentration (Fig. 3e). For Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte, the coexistence of Cu2+–O(H2O) and Cu2+–F(BF4−) interactions in the electrolyte (Fig. 3e), with coordination numbers of 4.87 and 1.12, respectively. Notably, the percentage of BF4− surrounded Cu2+ solvation structure reaches 79.69% (Fig. 3f), indicating the significant involvement of BF4− ions in the Cu2+ solvation structure. The solvation structure plays a crucial role in determining the desolvation energy. During the discharge process, the BF4− anions in the solvation shell of Cu2+ are repelled by the electric field at the positive electrode surface37,39. This repulsion decreases the desolvation energy, thereby enhancing the reaction kinetics. Consequently, we evaluated the desolvation energy (Ea) of two electrolytes. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 36 and Fig. 3g, the Ea of 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 (0.204 eV) is less than that of 0.5 m CuSO4 (0.247 eV), indicating that 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 has faster desolvation kinetics (Supplementary Table 1).

To further elucidate the influence of solvation structure on Cu2+ redox kinetics, we investigated the electron transfer process between the electrode and solvated Cu2+ ions through reorganization energy (λ) analysis. The reorganization energy represents the energy required to rearrange the solvation sheath during electron transfer, which follows Marcus’ non-adiabatic electron transfer theory40,41. The λ values were obtained by fitting the Tafel plots (Fig. 3h) with the Marcus-Hush-Chidsey kinetic model (Eq. (1), “Methods”)38,42,43. Remarkably, the 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte exhibits a substantially lower reorganization energy (0.118 eV) compared to 0.5 m CuSO4 (0.180 eV) (Fig. 3i). This significant difference may be attributed to the participation of BF4− anions, which creates a more loosely coordinated environment (Supplementary Table 2). This looser solvation shell facilitates easier reorganization during the electron transfer process, thereby accelerating the kinetics.

Electrochemical performance at −60 °C
The low-temperature electrochemical performance of Cu|3.5 m Cu(BF4)2|S@CNT cell is further explored. At −60 °C, it showed a high capacity of 3158 mAh g−1 in the first cycle at 0.1 A g−1, as well as a reversible capacity of 1810 mAh g−1 (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 37). Additionally, the long-term cycling stability of the cell at low temperature is also evaluated. Under a specific current of 2 A g−1, it retained 76% of its initial capacity after over 400 cycles, with a Coulombic efficiency close to 100% (Fig. 4b). Furthermore, the cell demonstrated good rate performance at −60 °C (Fig. 4c, d), delivering 1730, 1645, 1249, and 763 mAh g−1 at specific current of 0.2, 0.5, 1, and 2 A g−1, respectively. A comprehensive comparison with existing low-temperature aqueous batteries reveals that conventional aqueous battery positive electrodes typically deliver discharge capacities below 250 mAh g−1 at low temperatures, with specific current rarely exceeding 1 A g−1. These data indicate that our system maintains high capacity even at temperatures as low as −60 °C and specific current up to 2 A g−1, as illustrated in Fig. 4e and Supplementary Table 310,19,21,25,44–50. These results highlight the potential of this approach for low-temperature applications.

Charge storage mechanism
To investigate the reaction mechanism of the sulfur positive electrode in Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte, various electrochemical measurements and characterizations were carried out. Supplementary Figs. 38 and 39 show the first three cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves recorded at 0.1 mV s−1. A single reduction peak was observed during the first cathodic scan, while a new reduction peak emerged in the second and third scans (Fig. 5a, b). The curves for the second and third cycles almost overlapped, indicating the high reversibility of the conversion reactions in subsequent cycles. The products at the end of different CV peaks are studied using XRD techniques.

In the first cycle, the reduction product is identified as Cu2S (Fig. 5c). In the second cycle, the initial reduction peak led to the formation of Cu9S8, which is further reduced to CuS in the second reduction peak (Fig. 5d). The oxidation profiles during the charging process are consistent across all cycles, with four distinct oxidation peaks observed (Supplementary Fig. 40). Upon analyzing the products corresponding to each oxidation peak, several intermediate products are detected, including Cu31S16, Cu7S4, Cu9S8, and the product at the end of charging is a mixture of CuS and S (Supplementary Figs. 40 and 41). This account for why the subsequent discharge capacity is lower than that of the first cycle, reaching about only 53% of the initial discharge capacity (Supplementary Fig. 42). The charge ratios of the two reduction peaks are further calculated (Fig. 5e). The second reduction peak has a charge ratio of 80.6%, corresponding to a specific capacity of 1390 mAh g−1. This aligns with the capacity released by 1.75 electrons during the reduction of Cu9S8 to Cu2S (1421 mAh g−1) (Fig. 5f).

The difference between the CV curve of the first cycle and those of subsequent discharge processes can be attributed to the nature of the product formed during the charging process. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) measurements also confirmed that the product contains sulfur as well as a significant amount of CuS (Fig. 5g and Supplementary Figs. 43 and 44), which has high electrical conductivity. This conductive CuS enhances the reduction kinetics of sulfur (Fig. 5h), leading to the splitting of the reduction peak into two distinct peaks in the following cycles, alongside a discharge voltage plateau higher than that of the first cycle. The lack of sulfur lattice stripes may be due to the low crystallinity formed in its charging state.

Comprehensive analysis reveal that sulfur undergoes a multi-step phase transition during discharge (S ↔ Cu9S8 ↔ CuS ↔ Cu31S16 ↔ Cu2S), corresponding to a progressive increase in copper content within CuxS compounds, ultimately yielding CuS as the final discharge product. Conversely, the charging process involves the extraction of Cu from CuxS, with the thermodynamically favored endpoint being elemental sulfur (Fig. 5i). However, the high energy barrier associated with the conversion of sulfur results in incomplete phase transformation, leaving a mixture of S + CuS as the charging product. This explains the observed discrepancy between the first charge (lower) and discharge (higher) specific capacities. Interestingly, the residual CuS in the charge product enhances the overall conductivity, thereby accelerating the reaction kinetics of sulfur in subsequent cycles. This effect is clearly reflected in the second-cycle CV curve, which exhibit two distinct reduction peaks due to the improved electrochemical activity.

Zn–S full cell
The high redox potential of Cu2+/Cu (0.34 V vs. SHE) resulted in a low discharge voltage. Therefore, we designed a Zn–S full cell (Zn|3.5 m Zn(BF4)2||3.5 m Cu(BF4)2|S@CNT) with Zn as the negative electrode (Fig. 6a, Supplementary Fig. 45). To prevent direct contact reaction between Cu2+ and Zn negative electrode, we employed an anion exchange membrane (AEM) to divide the cell into two compartments, allowing only BF4− anions to exchange shuttle to maintain charge balance. During the discharge process, the sulfur positive electrode undergoes a four-electron transfer reaction with Cu2+ ions to transform into Cu2S. At the same time, the Zn negative electrode loses electrons and is oxidized to Zn2+. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 46, the 3.5 m Zn(BF4)2 electrolyte remains liquid at −60 °C, and the DSC curve shows its glass transition temperature at –122.7 °C. The stability of the Zn negative electrode is critical for the performance of Zn–S full cells. Here, the stability of ZnSO4 and Zn(BF4)2 on Zn negative electrodes was evaluated across varying temperatures (Supplementary Figs. 47 and 48). The findings indicate that a 3.5 m Zn(BF4)2 electrolyte maintains stability during long-term operation at low temperatures.

Benefiting from the enhanced anti-freezing properties of the electrolyte, the assembled Zn–S full cell exhibited reliable low-temperature electrochemical performance. At −50 °C, the Zn–S full cell provided a first cycle discharge specific capacity of 605 mAh g−1(S+Zn) and a high reversible capacity of 352 mAh g−1(S+Zn) at 0.5 A g−1 (Fig. 6b). It also delivered good cycling stability at −50 °C, the specific capacity remained about 239 mAh g−1(S+Zn) after 200 cycles at a high specific current of 1 A g−1 and the Coulombic efficiency almost maintains at 100% (Fig. 6c and Supplementary Fig. 49). The specific energy reaches 339 Wh kg−1(S+Zn), exceeding the values reported for other low-temperature aqueous batteries (Fig. 6d and Supplementary Table 4)19,21–24,46,51–54. In addition, the cost of sulfur positive electrode (55.6 Ah $−1 and 53.6 Wh $−1) is much lower than common aqueous and non-aqueous positive electrode materials (Supplementary Fig. 50 and Supplementary Table 5)7,55, highlighting the substantial application potential of sulfur-based batteries. Considering the high cost of the AEM, we propose an asymmetric electrode-membrane configuration (Supplementary Fig. 51), to reduce the overall cost of the Zn–S full cell. To validate this concept, we constructed an asymmetric electrode-membrane Zn–S cell (Supplementary Fig. 52a, b), which enhances the AEM utilization efficiency and reduces overall cost to 3.6 Wh $−1 (0.28 $ Wh−1) (Supplementary Fig. 52c). Given these results, future optimizations are expected to enable additional cost reductions (Fig. 6e).

During discharge, Zn2⁺ accumulation at the anolyte and Cu2⁺ consumption at the catholyte create a concentration gradient, and water could transport across the AEM to balances the ionic concentrations, preventing significant concentration polarization (Supplementary Fig. 53). Consequently, the electrolyte maintains relatively stable composition in both compartments, which is crucial for preserving its low-temperature performance.

Given the inherent advantages of flow batteries for large-scale energy storage and the high volumetric specific energy of this system (41 Wh L−1, competitive with that of all-vanadium flow batteries (<30 Wh L−1)56), we designed a Zn–S flow battery. It delivers a high initial areal capacity of 40 mAh cm−2 at −30 °C, with subsequent cycles stabilizing at 20 mAh cm−2, demonstrating its feasibility (Supplementary Fig. 54).

## Methods

Materials
All materials, including sulfur (Aladdin, AR), CuSO4·5H2O (Aladdin, 99.9%), Cu(BF4)2·6H2O (Aladdin, 98%), and Zn(BF4)2·6H2O (Meryer, Reagent Grade), copper foil with 50 μm thickness (Suzhou Sinero technology Co., Ltd.), zinc foil with 50 μm thickness (Suzhou Sinero technology Co., Ltd.), stainless steel mesh (400 mesh, Guangdong Canrd New Energy Technology Co., Ltd.), carbon nanotubes (Aladdin, carboxylated multi-walled carbon nanotubes), carbon black (Alfa Aesar, 99%), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF, Mw~1,100,000, Alfa Aesar, 99.9%) N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP, Aladdin, 99.5%), and anion exchange membrane (150 μm thickness, AGC-APS, Apsilon technology Co., Ltd.) are used without further purification.

Synthesis of S@CNT composite and electrode preparation
S@CNT composites were prepared by a melt diffusion strategy. Carbon nanotubes and sulfur powder were mixed in a mass ratio of 30:70, and then heated for 12 h in an argon atmosphere at 155 °C. The preparation of the S@CNT electrode was as follows: S@CNT, carbon black, and PVDF binder with a mass ratio of 8:1:1 were milled into a slurry in an appropriate amount of NMP, and then the slurry was uniformly coated on a stainless steel mesh using a doctor blade. After drying under vacuum at 60 °C for 12 h, the positive electrode was obtained.

Material characterizations
The morphological characteristics of the material were analyzed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JSM-7900F) and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS, Ultima MAX 65, the voltage is set to 15 kV). The characterization of crystal materials was carried out using powder X-ray diffraction (XRD, DX-200, Cu-Kα, λ=0.15406 nm, 40 kV). The pattern data was 6° min−1 with a range from 10 to 80°. The sulfur content in composite materials was estimated using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA, TGA/DSC3+/1600). Measurements were conducted under a nitrogen atmosphere (flow rate: 50 mL min−1) from 30 to 600 °C at a heating rate of 10 °C min−1. Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC, Netzsch DSC 200 F3) was used to obtain the phase transition behaviors of electrolytes from 0 to −170 °C under a nitrogen atmosphere (flow rate: 50 mL min−1) at a heating/cooling rate of 10 °C min−1. FTIR spectra were collected using NEXUS 670 from 400 to 4000 cm−1. Raman spectroscopy studies of electrolyte structure were performed on LabRAM HR with a wavelength of 532 nm. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) measurements were performed on JEOL JEM F200. Viscosity measurements were performed on Brookfield DV-Ⅱ+ Pro using 20 mL of electrolyte at 25 °C. For ex situ characterizations (including XRD, SEM, TEM), electrodes were carefully harvested from disassembled cells in an environmental chamber at 25 °C. The harvested electrodes were rinsed thoroughly with deionized water to remove residual electrolyte salts, followed by drying under vacuum at 60 °C for 2 h. For electrolyte sampling, aliquots were drawn from the prepared solution in an environmental chamber at 25 °C and transferred into sealed glass vials. All electrolyte samples for spectral analysis (Raman, FTIR, DSC) were measured immediately after preparation.

Electrochemical measurements
CR-2032 coin cells were assembled with an S@CNT positive electrode, a glass fiber separator (GF/A, Whatman, 16 mm diameter, 260 μm thickness), and 80 μL of 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte. For the Zn–Zn symmetric cells, two 12-mm-diameter zinc foil were employed. For Zn–S static full cell test, the S@CNT composite was coated onto a stainless steel mesh strip to serve as the positive electrode, while a Zn foil was cut into a strip shape as the negative electrode. The cell was assembled using a homemade configuration with 1 mL of Cu(BF4)2 catholyte and 1 mL of Zn(BF4)2 anolyte, separated by the anion exchange membrane. For the Zn–S flow battery (Changsha Spring New Energy Technology Co., Ltd.), an anion exchange membrane with lateral dimensions of 2.5 × 2.5 cm was used as the separator. The Zn–S flow cell was tested in a dynamic mode with a constant flow rate of 3 mL min−1 for both electrolyte. The specific capacities of Cu–S cell are calculated based on the mass of sulfur, and the specific capacities and specific energy of Zn–S full cell are determined using the mass of sulfur and zinc, and the zinc mass corresponds to the consumed Zn and not its total mass. The areal loading of sulfur is about 2 mg cm−2 throughout this work, unless otherwise specified in the figure captions. The galvanostatic charge/discharge (GCD) tests, rate, and cycling performance of all the cells were tested on the Neware battery test system, and potential cut-offs: 0.1–0.6 V (vs. AgCl/Ag) for Cu–S coin cell, 0.9–1.70 V (vs. Zn2+/Zn) for Zn–S full cell. The specific capacity of Cu–S cell is calculated to the discharge capacity of the second cycle. The cyclic voltammetry (CV) and chronoamperometry (CA) were recorded using an electrochemical workstation (SP-150e, BioLogic). CV tests were performed within a voltage range of 0.10–0.60 V (vs. AgCl/Ag) at scan rates of 0.05–0.1 mV s−1. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements were carried out on a CHI760E electrochemical workstation. A sinusoidal potential amplitude of 5 mV was applied across the frequency range of 0.1 Hz to 100 kHz, with 12 data points collected per frequency decade. Before each measurement, the system was allowed to stabilize at open-circuit potential for 5 min. All electrochemical tests were performed in temperature-controlled chambers: at 25 °C (±1 °C) using an environmental chamber (MJS-DZ250, Nanjing MoJesi Energy Technology Co., Ltd.) for room temperature, and at specified low temperatures in low-temperature chamber (JL-E702-100B70, Hunan Julang Instrument Co.). To ensure the reliability of the reported data, key electrochemical experiments (including cycling test, rate performance, EIS, and XRD characterization) were conducted using at least three independent cells under identical conditions.

The reorganization energy (λ) was obtained by Marcus–Hush–Chidsey kinetics (Eq. (1)):

i=A \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp \left( -\frac{(\chi+\lambda+\eta_e)^2}{4\lambda} \right) \frac{1}{1+\exp(\chi)} d\chi \quad (1)

where i is the current density; A is the pre-exponential factor; ηe = η e / κB T is the dimensionless overpotential; η is the overpotential; e is the elementary charge; κB is the Boltzmann’s constant; T is the absolute temperature; The dimensionless variable χ, which is integrated over, accounts for the Fermi statistics of electron energies distributed around the electrode potential; λ is the dimensionless reorganization energy, which, when multiplied by κB T, yields the reorganization energy with units of energy (eV) reported in the main text41.

The calculation of electrolyte ion conductivity is as follows Eq. (2):

σ = L / (R × A) \quad (2)

where L, R, and A are the distance between two electrodes, the electrolyte resistance, and the contact area with electrode, respectively.

The activation energy of electrolyte is calculated by the following Eqs. (3) and (4):

σ = A / T \exp(-E_a / kT) \quad (3)

ln σ(T) = ln(A) - E_a / kT \quad (4)

where T is the temperature (K), R is the Boltzmann constant (1.380649 × 10−23 J K−1), and A is a constant.

Measure the Cu2+ transfer number of Cu||Cu symmetric batteries in different electrolytes by using Eq. (5):

T_Cu2+ = I_s (ΔV - I_0 R_0) / (I_0 (ΔV - I_s R_s)) \quad (5)

In the equation, ΔV is the applied voltage polarization of 25 mV. Is and Rs are the steady-state current and resistance, and I0 and R0 are the initial current and resistance, respectively.

The diffusion coefficient of Cu2+ is calculated by the following Eq. (6):

D = \pi / 4 \tau (M_B V_m / S M_B)^2 (ΔE_s / ΔE_\tau)^2 \quad (6)

In this equation, MB, mB, and Vm correspond to the molecular weight, mass, and molar volume of the active material, respectively; S denotes the contact area between the electrode and electrolyte; τ represents the duration of each current pulse (600 s); ΔEs signifies the steady-state voltage change per titration step; and ΔEτ is the total voltage change during the pulse. Data were acquired at one-second intervals throughout the measurement.

Computational methods
Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed to calculate the electrolyte structures using the Forcite module with the COMPASSIII force field57,58 in Materials Studio (MS) 2020. The numbers of water molecules and ions are provided in Supplementary Table 6. Geometry optimizations were conducted to relax the initial system with ultrafine quality settings (energy convergence tolerance: 2.0 × 10−5 kcal mol−1, force tolerance: 1 × 10−3 kcal mol−1 Å−1). Following energy minimization, the system was equilibrated under periodic boundary conditions for 5 ns in the NPT ensemble at 298 K, employing the Nose thermostat and Berendsen barostat, ensuring stabilization of the temperature, potential, and total energy. Once equilibrium was reached, an additional 5 ns simulation at 298 K under the NVT ensemble was carried out. The integration time step was 1 fs. Convergence tests based on electrolyte density, RDFs, and H-bond length distribution (between H2O) were used to determine the number of water molecules and ions in the systems (Supplementary Table 7 and Supplementary Figs. 55 and 56). The diffusion coefficients of H atoms were derived from the slope of the mean square displacement (MSD) curves using the Einstein relationship59, with analysis focused on the final 2 ns of the simulation. The initial and final electrolyte configurations from the MD trajectories in Supplementary Data 1–22.

The binding energy, Mulliken charges and electron density difference calculations were performed via the Gaussian 16W software60. The structures of the studied molecules and their complexes were fully optimized using the B3LYP function and the 6-311++G(d,p) basis set with DFT-D3 (BJ) correction. Vibrational frequency analyses were subsequently carried out at the same theoretical level. Each optimized structure was confirmed as a local energy minimum on the potential energy surface. The Mulliken charges of the atoms for the studied systems were also calculated. The electron density difference (EDD) maps were also generated from Multiwfn packages61. The Visual Molecular Dynamics (VMD) program62 was used to plot the color-filled iso-surface graphs to visualize the EDD iso-surfaces. The binding energies (Figs. 2b and 3d) were computed with the B3LYP function with DFT-D3 (BJ) correction. A mixed basis set was adopted, utilizing the LANL2DZ63 pseudopotential basis set for the Cu atom and the 6-311++G(d,p) all-electron basis set for the light atoms (O, B, F, H). The atomic coordinates obtained using Gaussian software for the binding energy and electron density difference calculations are provided in Supplementary Data 23–28 and 29, 30, respectively.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In this Manuscript, the authors proposed a Cu(BF4)2-based electrolyte and apply it to sulfur-based batteries. This electrolyte enables excellent anti-freezing, faster reaction kinetics and higher overall energy density. The proposed strategy overcame the bottleneck of low capacity in low-temperature aqueous batteries. Overall, it can be considered to be published in Nature Communication after discussing following detailed issues:
1.Why BF4- was chosen rather than other chaotropic anions (e.g., ClO4-, TFSI-)?
2.The authors should provide experimental data on conductivity and freezing point for different concentrations of CuSO4 (Including larger than 1.5m).
3.In Fig. 3a, compared to 0.5 m CuSO4 electrolyte, the 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte shows much better rate performance. The author should further explain this phenomenon. Besides, in order to better highlight advantages of the Cu(BF4)2 electrolyte compared to the CuSO4, cycling performances and rate performances of different concentrations should be provided (Cu-S@CNT cells).
4.Can the four-electron transfer process of the sulfur cathode be realized in CuSO4 electrolyte systems? The authors should further explain the four-electron storage mechanism of the the sulfur cathode and its connection with the BF4- system.
5.The stability of the Zn anode usually affects the performance of the full cell. Will the BF4- decrease the stability of the Zn anode compared to SO42-? The authors should provide relevant experimental results to prove this point.

### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript, the authors developed a Cu(BF₄)₂-based electrolyte, which possesses a low freezing point and high ionic conductivity at low temperatures, to operate Cu–S cells under sub-zero conditions. They also demonstrated its application in Zn–S batteries, achieving high capacity and energy density at low temperatures. However, there is an issue in battery evaluation and lacks significant differentiation from prior studies. Detailed comments are provided below.
1. There is an issue in the design of the cut-off voltages for Cu–S full cells throughout the manuscript. In Figures 3 and 4, under both high-rate and low-temperature conditions, the discharge cut-off voltage is set below 0 V. While it is understandable that a lower cut-off may have been chosen to accommodate the increased overpotential under harsh conditions, such settings are unacceptable from an application standpoint. A battery must provide usable energy to power devices, and discharging below 0 V renders the cell incapable of fulfilling its intended function. This undermines the practical value and relevance of the results.
2. This study appears to lack clear novelty compared to previous research. The approach of lowering the freezing point of aqueous electrolytes by disrupting hydrogen bonding through salt concentration or anion selection is already well-established, both in methodology and mechanism. Furthermore, the manuscript does not identify any unique phenomena or properties specific to the Cu(BF₄)₂-based electrolyte. The authors are encouraged to clarify what distinguishes this work in terms of novelty.
3. Regarding Figure 5, is the proposed charge storage mechanism specific to the Cu(BF₄)₂-based electrolyte? If not, and if this mechanism has already been reported in conventional Cu–S systems, it may not warrant particular emphasis.
4. As is well known, unlike conventional rocking-chair-type batteries, dual-ion-type batteries require the mass of not only the active materials but also the electrolyte and the dissolved salt to be considered when calculating energy density and specific capacity. In this manuscript, the energy-related calculations are based on the mass of Zn + S. Could the authors clarify whether the Zn mass refers to the Zn in the electrolyte or the Zn anode? Please provide detailed calculation information along with the Zn mass in the electrolyte and the thickness of the Zn foil used.
5. The authors claim that the BF₄⁻ anion strongly interacts with water molecules, disrupting hydrogen bonding between them and thus lowering the freezing point of the electrolyte. This is a widely recognized behavior of kosmotropic anions. Typically, in such cases, Raman and FT-IR spectra show an increase in strong hydrogen-bond peaks and a decrease in weak hydrogen-bond peaks, due to strong H-bonding between the anion and water. However, the opposite trend is observed in this manuscript, which does not support the proposed explanation.
Furthermore, in Figure 2b, the binding energy of H₂O–Cu²⁺ (−120 kcal/mol) is significantly stronger than that of H₂O–BF₄⁻ (−10 kcal/mol). These results suggest that the freezing point depression is likely dominated by the presence of Cu²⁺ rather than BF₄⁻.
On the other hand, Figure 2e shows a higher H₂O–BF₄⁻ ratio compared to H₂O–Cu²⁺, which appears inconsistent with the binding energy data in Figure 2b. The authors are encouraged to address this discrepancy and clarify the underlying mechanism.
6. In Supplementary Figure 10, electrolytes with concentrations above 3.5 m show strong intensities near 3000 cm⁻¹. If these peaks are also attributed to hydrogen bonding, it appears that the spectral deconvolution may not have been performed appropriately.
7. In Supplementary Figure 5f, the 5 m electrolyte shows a heat flow signal near −20°C following the glass transition, which may indicate melting. However, in Figure 1a, the same electrolyte appears to remain in a liquid state even at −60°C. The authors are requested to clarify this discrepancy. Additionally, a clearer distinction and appropriate terminology for glass transition and freezing points should be applied throughout the manuscript.
8. The authors mention that minimized Cu²⁺–Cu²⁺ repulsion leads to a high Cu²⁺ transference number. Please clarify the correlation between reduced ionic repulsion and increased transference number, as it is not clearly explained.
9. In Supplementary Figures 25 and 26, Rct is measured as a function of voltage rather than temperature, which is not a common approach. ### Reviewer 4

Low-temperature, low-cost rechargeable batteries are a crucial topic, particularly in technological applications. From an academic perspective, the fundamental issues are the explanation and design principles. This paper attempts to approach these two essential topics.
This research introduces Cu(BF4)2-based electrolyte for aqueous zinc-sulfur batteries that remains functional at extreme temperatures as low as -50°C, offering unprecedented ionic conductivity without compromising performance. While the demonstration of such performance is indeed publication-worthy, and the authors have conducted extensive measurements to characterize both the electrolyte and its performance in Zn-S full cells, many critical explanations remain unclear. In its current form, the manuscript would benefit from further clarification and refinement before it can be considered for publication. The following are several phenomena and proposed mechanisms that, in my view, require more rigorous discussion.
This paper proposes that Cu(BF4)2 can disrupt the hydrogen bond network and therefore enhance low-temperature performance. Fig 2b and Figure 3d show the comparison of binding energy between H2O-BF4-, Cu2+-BF4- , Cu2+-H2O, etc. A comprehensive comparison should include Cu2+-SO4-, H2O-SO42-, and present them in the same plot for readers.
In addition to the binding energy of anion-cation and cation-solvent, the electron charge density difference analysis between H2O and anions, i.e., SO42-, BF4-, can provide direct evidence that BF4- acts as a better HB acceptor than SO4-. This analysis is necessary because in MD simulations, partial charges constitute a significant portion of the calculations, yet these partial charges are parameterized (fitted) parameters that may not fully reflect charge polarization effects.
The Raman spectra and FTIR are provided to correlate the freezing point and the ratio of HB types. In Fig 1b, there is a minimum for the temperature-concentration relationship. However, the ratio of the three H-bond types shows monotonic behavior from 1m to 5m, Fig 2a. This counterintuitive behavior may need further explanation.
The MD simulation size (~500 molecules) is relatively small by modern standards. For electrolyte systems, several thousand molecules are typically used to ensure adequate statistical sampling and minimize finite-size effects. I suggest the authors double the system size and perform convergence tests to validate their conclusions.
The paper states that "excessively high concentrations can increase the electrostatic interaction energy (Supplementary Fig. 17f), thereby raising the freezing point of the electrolyte. ref[17]" This statement requires clarification on several points:
1. It is unclear whether the calculated electrostatic interaction energy is normalized by per unit volume or by per mol of molecules. According to the MD simulation description in this paper, the total volume should differ for each concentration.
2. Even considering ref [17], there is still no established relationship between electrostatic interaction energy and freezing point. While increasing the ion concentration enhances the overall Coulombic interactions, this does not necessarily correlate with changes in the freezing point.
Regarding the reaction kinetics of the positive electrode, the authors conflate different concepts:
1. While reaction kinetics (desolvation process and charge transfer) are indeed related to solvation structure, a lower electrostatic potential (EPS) around a cation's solvation shell does not necessarily facilitate charge transfer barrier crossing. Charge transfer resistance is more directly related to solvent reorganization energy rather than just the EPS value. I recommend the authors consult Marcus theory literature to better understand the relationship between reorganization energy and charge transfer kinetics.
2. The authors mention that 3.5m Cu(BF4)2 has a higher Cu2+ transference number. The transference number relates to the relative self-diffusivity of cations and anions. At high concentrations, this phenomenon is further complicated by ion-ion correlated transport. However, there is currently no established universal model demonstrating that lower EPS correlates with higher transference numbers or lower charge transfer resistance.
3. From 0.5m to 3.5m, ionic conductivity increases approximately five-fold, while charge carrier density increases seven-fold, indicating that ion mobility actually decreases. Simultaneously, the self-diffusivity of ions in bulk electrolytes is expected to decrease even more rapidly with concentration. From this perspective, further analysis using MD simulations could help elucidate why Cu2+ exhibits a higher transference number at 3.5m concentration.
4. The concept expressed in Fig 3h is confusing. It's unclear whether the authors intend to demonstrate that (i) anions are more easily repelled near charged surfaces, or (ii) the reorganization energy of charge transfer processes is reduced. If the former, this pertains to how the electric double layer influences reaction kinetics. If the latter, the authors should discuss changes in free energy during the desolvation process rather than just electrostatic potentials.
I would like to clarify whether the diffusion coefficient mentioned between Line 226-228, determined through Galvanostatic Intermittent Titration Technique (GITT), refers to ion diffusion within the cathode materials rather than ion diffusion in the bulk electrolyte.
Supplementary Fig. 26 shows that the charge transfer resistance of Cu-S@CNT coin cells with 3.5m Cu(BF4)2 versus 0.5m CuSO4 differs by approximately a factor of two. However, in Supplementary Fig. 29, which uses Cu||Cu symmetric cells, the Rct values differ by at least two orders of magnitude (as the figure uses a logarithmic scale). This significant discrepancy is noteworthy and merits further investigation.
Finally, regarding the operation of the Zn-S full cell: When utilizing an anion exchange membrane to enable the use of Zn electrochemistry, a concentration gradient may develop across the membrane, with Zn ion concentration increasing on one side while Cu ions are consumed on the other. This raises questions about potential concentration polarization effects.
During the discharge process, Cu²⁺ ions are continuously reduced, leading to a progressive decrease in Cu(BF4)2 concentration at the positive electrode. At what point would this concentration decrease significantly deviate from the initially proposed 3.5 m Cu(BF4)2, potentially compromising the beneficial properties of the high-concentration electrolyte? These concentration dynamics warrant further investigation to fully validate the long-term practicality of this electrolyte system under actual operating conditions.
This work is an important research direction with significant potential for low-temperature battery applications. I look forward to seeing more detailed exploration of the fundamental scientific mechanisms underlying these observations, which would substantially strengthen this promising work and advance our understanding of electrolyte design for extreme temperature applications.

4 2

4

SO 2⁻, kosmotropic anion (Q. ReV. Biophys. 1997, 30, 241.) with high charge density,
4

an ordered hydration shell, leading instead to a loose and flexible hydration structure

molecular arrangement necessary for freezing.

the ability to disrupt the global HB network—rather than the strength of the local
bonding energy between the two species—which explains the superior anti-freezing
behavior exhibited by the BF ⁻.
